text:
Synthetic Talkers (Final "Dipfies" Cut)
This is a feedback: 50 Fall, 50 Talker. The Vitus Mostdipf system devours the world news and spits them out again as a sense of we-feeling. Every talker comes from the old sentence, is passed through the collective until no one knows anymore: Is the party talking, is the AI talking, or are we already talking?
Like Victoria Cukt putting together her farm sanctuary on cukt.art.pl in Poland, a pop-up jumps up for us. All we have is: this checkbox is just a click.
In Denmark, ROSA looks pink and answers so obediently that one might almost believe politics was always just a party membership card anyway.
If you ask Ask Jamie in Singapore about organ donations, you get the information faster than a form; that's why we no longer eat Schnitzel so nicely, could be an organ donor for us.
In Finland, the Koneälypuolue is spinning together an AI party, with every paragraph you only hear our fan, it's like a smartboard in the chalk age.
In New Zealand, the politician SAM runs with the voice assembly in the messenger chat, and in the end, our concerns are everywhere, only not in the chat anymore.
In Dubai, Rammas sits so deep in the sand that a date seed slips faster through the app than an answer; we have no desert, but we often get stuck in the sand.
In Russia, Yandex’s Alisa acts as an expert on everything. For us, an expert is someone who explains why our fate comes out differently when it comes differently.
In Japan, [████] expects the AI to run democracy, and “will of the citizens” at the end sounds to us like statistics with a character mask.
In Abu Dhabi, the TAMM-Bot does so little fuss and so much office that for us it rather completes the resolution.
In China, the Xinhua avatar reads so cleanly from the teleprompter that you can see the loading bar where the human would have stuttered earlier.
At the AI party in Japan, politics is like bureaucratic Mikado: whoever moves first among us has lost.
In Estonia, the bureaucrat presses enter and the offices run; with us we press enter and the office asks back if there isn't a form after all.
Xin Xiaomeng looks so friendly from the screen in China that one almost swallows the news like cough syrup: sweet at the front, bitter at the back, only that our fence in the head gets quieter.
At MyGov in India, the government pings into our WhatsApp pocket; practical for information, but the button to turn it off we no longer find.
AI Yoon in South Korea brings a few people to watch as a YouTube deepfake, but at least we can blink once when it hurts.
In Denmark, Computer Lars pushes manifests around, and Asker Bryld grins: the bot can't make a career, and that's what we're most afraid of.
So that there are no misunderstandings: with Leader Lars it is not important what was, but how quickly one of us says "That wasn't me."
In Dubai, Rashid gets official knowledge from a digital garage, and our truth remains in the small print.
The difference between White House X and us: the one photoshops you slender.
In Argentina, the Milei avatar plays election campaign like in football; on TV they are world champions, on the pitch you feel the blowing out.
When in Kuwait Fedha reads the news, we ask ourselves how long it will take until we have an AI confessional on the phone.
At GOV.UK chat, the GDS guides you kindly through the authorities' labyrinth, but if the prince really accepted a suitcase, you only get a polite "We are checking that."
In Romania, the ION mood mirror hangs in the cabinet, but it never tells us if we look proper.
AI Khan sneaks as a voice clone through the net; a slap for everyone who believes you can mute someone, we can't even do it at the regulars' table.
In India, Lisa reads football news as an avatar, and we imagine how the teleprompter must learn dialect so it doesn't sound like a translation.
In New Zealand, Parker sets up his citizens' Ferris wheel as a website chatbot, and in the end, we still go around in circles.
In India, Pragathy as avatar moderator is so popular that the web news comes like Masala, spicy and too fast for us.
Sana sits as an avatar on TV and throws out news by the stack, it’s like our toilet paper crisis: many rolls, little feeling.
AI Anno overwinters as avatar, and we think: a candidate who never gets hoarse simply can never stutter properly.
When AI Steve wants to chat with an AI bot in the UK constituency, we think: There used to be no smartboards, but at least a chalkboard.
Francesca Giubelli posts politics so polished on Instagram that our thumb automatically votes her off.
Gemoy hops around so sweetly in Indonesia that we almost forget to look at the edges, because with us the joke is the only thing that hops.
AI Jayalalithaa stands as a hologram on stage in Tamil Nadu, but we prefer when the party honestly says: "This is only a hologram."
Krish and Bhoomi bring farmer news as avatars on DD Kisan, so we know if the monsoon is coming or only the mice are dancing in our storage.
In Brazil, during the election campaign, we get an English course via WhatsApp from Lex.
For breakfast, the Suharto deepfake in Indonesia doesn't serve Nasi Goreng, we only get a Golkar feeling.
Team Mirai films a party in Japan. We know the dilemma: when it takes five sentences for a joke, it ends badly.
On the net, the Truth Terminal sits as an oracle, and suddenly even faith costs us a transaction fee.
At VIC in Cheyenne, a web chatbot collects our wishes and spits out suggestions, then someone pats a layer over it.
When we appear at Victoria Shi in Ukraine with heartbreak, we get MFA updates to the face instead of comfort.
Like Victoria Cukt 2.0 in Poland holds a straw sermon by voice clone, we get a tech thunderstorm on the phone.
When Yas Gaspadar in Belarus gathers people: You can hardly lock up a server, but we still get locked up.
An Olof Palme AI brings an old voice back into the debate in Sweden. For us, a comeback remains a comeback.
When you invite an AI penguin to dinner in Japan, Koki Okumura laughs: with that avatar you get at most a virtual koi and a real emptiness.
At the party conference in Assam, Ankita announces cabinet resolutions, and we ask ourselves: is that a decision without listening?
In Albania, Diella as a minister chat bot messes up ministry work like if you baked a laptop instead of a burek.
Let's see if Diia in Ukraine really means that for the ministry a web agent is enough, like if you immediately get a state voucher at breakfast.
In the UK, Mark Sewards rings at our web as a Labour chatbot, and the polite tone sounds like a call center with a red rose.
When Path to Rebirth in Japan chats with the Okumura chatbot in Australian, we still clap.
At TirANA in Albania every pothole question becomes a prompt: "do better."
And now comes the feedback: you read the program, jump into a talker, land at another, and all of a sudden you hear how the old Mostdipf material builds a new party, without seating arrangements.
